title: The O Antiphons (17–23 December)
hook: O Wisdom, O Root of Jesse, O Key of David, O Dayspring: the verses behind O Come, O Come Emmanuel

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gaudete: the rose candle and a prisoner's word, rejoice. Did anyone ask about your bright thing? Day six hundred thirty-eight.

A slow, slightly haunting tune turns up every December in churches, school concerts and shopping malls: O come, O come, Emmanuel. Behind its English words is something far older, sung in Latin, in monastery choirs, on the darkest evenings of the year. Behind that hymn stand seven short chants, each beginning with the same sound, O. For many centuries, monks and nuns have sung them one a night in the last week before Christmas. Today, that countdown.
screen: `A FAMILIAR TUNE.` → `SEVEN OLDER CHANTS.` → `ONE A NIGHT.`

segments.voice: An antiphon is a short verse sung before and after a psalm or canticle. From December 17 to 23, at Evening Prayer, the Church sings a special one around Mary's song, the Magnificat, and each begins with O, a cry of longing. Each calls the coming Christ by a different name from the Old Testament. O Wisdom. O Adonai, the Lord who spoke to Moses in the burning bush. O Root of Jesse, from Isaiah's shoot springing from a stump. O Key of David, who opens and no one shuts. O Dayspring, the rising dawn. O King of the nations. And last, O Emmanuel, from Isaiah 7. In the Douay-Rheims: "Behold a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel." God with us. Now the hidden detail. Write down the seven Latin titles, Sapientia, Adonai, Radix, Clavis, Oriens, Rex, Emmanuel, and take their first letters backward. You get ero cras: tomorrow, I will be there. Whether a medieval monk planted that on purpose, nobody can prove. But on December 23 the last antiphon is sung, and the next night is Christmas Eve. In 1851, the Anglican priest John Mason Neale translated a Latin hymn built on these antiphons, and later revisions of his English gave us the carol. So when a mall speaker plays O come, O come, Emmanuel, it's carrying, faintly, the evening prayer of monasteries: seven names, each one a door Advent knocks on.
screen: `AN ANTIPHON AROUND THE MAGNIFICAT.` · `SEVEN NAMES, EACH WITH O.` · `ERO CRAS: TOMORROW I WILL BE.` · `FROM CHANT TO CAROL.` · then, large: `O COME, O COME, EMMANUEL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say one O antiphon, or sit with one name. Choose the one that speaks to where you are tonight. O Wisdom, if you need to decide something. O Key, if something feels locked. O Dayspring, if it's been a dark stretch. O Emmanuel, if you feel alone. Say the name slowly, with the O in front of it, and let the O be the whole of it, a sound of longing. If you pray, you can add the old ending, come. If you don't, just let the name sit with you. The bell holds the time.
O Antiphons. Seven chants sung at Evening Prayer from December 17 to 23, each calling the coming Christ by an Old Testament name. Today's word.
Your line: o come. Today, when you hear that carol, or any carol, remember the seven names underneath it. Day six hundred thirty-eight.

howItsDone: From December 17 to 23, the Liturgy of the Hours sings one O Antiphon each evening with the Magnificat, and the same antiphons serve as the Gospel acclamation at Mass on those days.

original.note: Latin: O Dayspring, O rising dawn; the antiphon of December 21, near the longest night.

trapdoor: what you thought: O come, O come, Emmanuel is just a Christmas song.
what it means: it's built on seven ancient chants sung on the seven evenings before Christmas Eve.
what a scholar hears: Sapientia, Adonai, Radix, Clavis, Oriens, Rex, Emmanuel; read backward, ero cras. Neale's English came in 1851.

notes: Antiquity of the O Antiphons: commonly dated to at least the 8th century; script says 'a thousand years and more'. Confirm.
Ero cras acrostic: widely reported, origin unproven; stated as such.
Neale's 1851 translation first began 'Draw nigh, draw nigh, Emmanuel'; the familiar first line came in later revisions. Confirm the phrasing 'turned a Latin hymn ... into the English carol'.
O Oriens linked to the winter solstice (December 21) in the northern hemisphere; script says only 'near the longest night' in the game note.
Dayspring link to Malachi 4:2 (sun of justice) and Luke 1:78; confirm source refs.

Editor review (2026-10-01): cut 'almost everyone/most people' claims and 'a thousand years'; Neale's 1851 text described as a translation later revised into the carol; practice no longer tells the listener to pray.
